approachQuestion.prompt:
Reverse a Route Record

A route is stored as a singly linked list of node objects. Return the head reference for the same nodes in reverse order. The list may be empty. You must not change node values or create, remove, or replace nodes; only next references may change.

Constraints: 0 <= n <= 200,000. Each node has an integer value and one next reference. The input is a finite acyclic list. The caller provides the head reference and expects one head reference (or null) as output.

Example 1: 4 -> 9 -> 2 -> null returns the original node chain 2 -> 9 -> 4 -> null.
Example 2: 7 -> null returns that same node, still ending in null.
Example 3: null returns null. Which method correctly returns the reversed chain for every allowed input while using the least additional storage?
constraints: The input is a finite acyclic singly linked list with at most 200,000 nodes.
Preserve every original node object and value; change only next references.
The input head and returned head are references, not copied node records.

options.text: Walk forward with a previous reference and a current reference. Save current.next before redirecting it to previous, then advance both references; return previous after the walk.
options.feedback: Saving the next node before redirecting the current link keeps the unprocessed suffix reachable, including when the walk reaches the final node.

options.text: Recursively reverse the suffix after the first node, then link the suffix's former first node back to the first node and clear the first node's next reference.
options.feedback: This rewires the original nodes correctly, but the nested calls retain one frame per node. The iterative version can perform the same rewiring without retaining that growing call history.

options.text: Keep the links unchanged and swap values from the two ends toward the middle.
options.feedback: The node objects remain in their original order, and their values are changed. For nodes A(4) -> B(9), this returns A(9) -> B(4), but the required result is B(9) -> A(4).

options.text: Scan from the head. For each node, set its next reference to the previously visited node, then advance by reading the current node’s next reference.
options.feedback: Changing current.next destroys the link to the unprocessed suffix before it is saved. On 4 -> 9 -> 2, the first change makes node 4 point to null, so advancing through current.next ends the walk and loses nodes 9 and 2.

feedback.reason: A node's original successor must remain reachable until it has been saved, and every original node must become reachable from the returned head in reverse order.
details: Keep a reference to the already reversed prefix and one to the not-yet-processed suffix. Before changing the current node's next reference, save that successor. Point the current node back to the prefix, then advance the prefix and continue from the saved successor. When no unprocessed node remains, the prefix begins the result.

Save the original successor before reversing next, or the unprocessed suffix becomes unreachable. The previous pointer owns the reversed prefix and current owns the untouched suffix. At null, previous is the complete new head.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed iterative-three-reference-reversal method described after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Count the returned head reference as output. The input nodes are supplied and are not auxiliary storage.
constraints: Use the worst-case bound over all allowed list lengths.
Include temporary references and call-stack storage, if any; exclude input nodes and the single-reference output.

feedback.reason: One visit per node reverses links with fixed references.
details: Each node is visited once. Before changing its link, the method saves its successor; the invariant is that previous is the reversed prefix and current begins the untouched suffix. At completion the suffix is empty and previous is the new head. Only a fixed number of references are retained, and the algorithm is iterative.
For a list of n nodes, every next reference must be redirected to produce the reversed chain, so the worst case requires visiting all n nodes. The loop processes each node a constant number of times.
The method retains only previous, current, and the saved successor. It uses no recursion; supplied nodes and the output head reference are excluded.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This fits the recursive alternative's call stack in the worst case, not the fixed iterative method.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Repeated predecessor searches can be quadratic; the fixed method advances through the list only once.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: For arbitrary input order, links across the list must be inspected and changed; one constant number of operations cannot process every node.
Iterative pointer algorithm; the fixed number of machine-word references is auxiliary storage. Input nodes and returned head reference are excluded.

methodReveal.title: Reverse each link as you advance
methodReveal.description: Keep a reference to the already reversed prefix and one to the not-yet-processed suffix. Before changing the current node's next reference, save that successor. Point the current node back to the prefix, then advance the prefix and continue from the saved successor. When no unprocessed node remains, the prefix begins the result.
